sections.title: Chairman's Chat
sections.content:
Tam (AKA Glorious Leader) reports

“You're only here for a short visit. Don't hurry. Don't worry. And be sure to smell the flowers along the way.”

Some stunning flights this month, very very good to see, well done to all involved. I am still in awe of people covering these distances! For the huge distances you had to be prepared to travel, south mainly.  As I write these flights have put the DHPC back at the top of the clubs in the XC league, proper order we would say of course. Chris Kay’s article in this newsletter shows that you don’t have to travel far to have brilliant days - 4 peaks in the central Dales in 1 flight is a fantastic day out in anyone’s book!  I would die of happiness at such a flight.  However, I am also reminded that our sport is not just about colossal distances, even for the sky gods. There are few flights that I have walked away from after packing up where I do not grin at the thought of what I’ve been doing, and the sheer joy of doing what we do - out in beautiful countryside, often stunning views, a laugh with mates- so what if you haven’t flown 50k, 100k, whatever. As Jockie Sanderson always says - the best pilot is the one having the most fun. Be grateful for what our sport gives you, we are very privileged indeed, and to quote another great sportsman, Walter Hagen  - "You're only here for a short visit. Don't hurry. Don't worry. And be sure to smell the flowers along the way." 

I am delighted to say that Chris Timson took up the club offer to part fund a club member to attend the BHPA repackers course as a first step to becoming a qualified repacker. Having our own repacker will be a real boon for the club and reduce our dependence on purely commercial providers for the club repack, but also give members someone local to use if they want to pay for a repack. Many thanks Chris, we wish you well with the course and qualifying.

We have some dates coming up that you should have in your diaries. Although not holding the “Fly In”, we ARE having the slightly downgraded Dales Camping W/e. Basically the fly in without the marquee. Given decent weather we will organise tasks, coaching etc. Even without decent weather there will be the camp fire, BBQs and loads of parabollox with your clubmates to enjoy. It is essentially a social w/e for club members, indeed any flyers, families, pets, hangers on etc.

Venue: Lodge Park, Langcliffe. BD24 9LT .  4th -  6th September. Book direct with the campsite through Pitchup.

Also coming up is the Farmers’ Dinner at The Knights Table, Stainforth. BD24 0DP, on October 17th.  Here we host the farmers whose good will we rely on for our flying. The club doesn’t pay any (well, many) site fees, and instead invites all our farmers to this slap up meal each year. It’s a good night and great food for around £25 per head. The menus will be out soon and we will put booking details on the website and advertise through the social channels. More members attending would be great to see.

Later in the month (around 25th), the BHPA will release its response to the CAA  “Consultation on a Proposed Electronic Conspicuity Mandate in the UK”. All BHPA members will be encouraged to use this response as a basis for giving their own response to the consultation, for which the deadline is 22nd Sept.

Finally, congratulations to Jordan, who has now fully taken over the reins at Active Edge. We look forward to a close relationship with the school, through which many of our members have come of course. Jordan will also be looking to continue the kit side of business and will be selling a wide range of equipment - a good port of call if you are looking for something. I’ll leave it to Jordan to let you know what he’s got when he’s ready.

Fly safe everyone, hopefully see you on a hill soon.

sections.title: Sites and News
sections.content:
The 12th August is known to some as The Glorious Twelfth - the start of the grouse shooting season.  It is one of the busiest days in the shooting season, which for grouse, lasts until early December.  

Grouse shooting is big business - providing a significant income for landowners, and supporting the livelihoods of many people who live and work in the Dales. It also represents the greatest threat to restrictions on our flying sites.  We may not consider it to be particularly 'glorious' because it imposes seasonal limitations on our flying sites.  However, we share the countryside and it is vital that we respect the wishes of others.  The club is unable to negotiate access to some places because of shooting, and we have agreements in other places (such as Stags Fell and Nappa Scar) which are vulnerable if we don’t get it right.

The partridge and pheasant seasons (which start in September and October respectively, and run to the end of January) are less likely to interact with flying, but we need to remain mindful of any shooting activity at flying sites.

Please note the restrictions shown on the Home and Sites pages.  We want to stay safe, and we don't want to lose a site.

Nappa Scar and Stags Fell - No XC flights between 12 Aug - 31 Dec.
Kilnsley - Site closed from 1st August to 31st December. No flying during this period.
Addleborough - No flying during the months of Sep - Nov unless prior approval obtained.
Wether Fell – Shoots happen at various times in autumn and winter, usually on a Saturday.  If we get the dates we'll let you know.  It's the area NE of take-off, along the Cam High Road.  If you see the obvious signs of a shoot - please avoid by staying to the SW.

sections.title: Safety: The mental game
sections.content:
Rob Urselmann reports

Sometimes a day just isn’t for you. Sunday 3 Aug was that for me.

Haven flown little and with a 5* forecast, I was keen to go out and a gaggle of seven pilots set out for Windbank. However, whilst active, I wasn’t quite firing on all cylinders. Not poorly, just a few % below 100 and a bit low on energy. Even I barely noticed. Strike 1.

The promised booming sky didn’t deliver, and the play was purely thermic. People launched, some stayed up, some quickly bombed and had a hard slog back up.  Eventually I launched in a promising gust, but immediately sank below the ridgeline. I found a thermal coming up the ridge immediately W of TO. Now, I always press during any coaching that thermalling below the ridge line close to the ridge is very high risk in case you drop out on the turn toward the hill, so listening to myself I figure-8’d until above the ridge… just above the ridge line. As I cleared the ridge turning away from the hill I was deciding whether to stick another S turn in or to full circle. I recall having this flash of ‘this is tight’ but I stuck with the turn…and promptly lost it anyhow … facing the hill. Thank god I was at least above the ridge line, albeit with little clearance. I ended up making a rather rapid “top landing”, caught my foot and face planted. The damage, apart from my pride, seemed to be only a torn radio headset line and a bit of a bruised knee and thumb*.  I sorted my gear, balled up and walked back to the front. Nothing serious but Strike 2.

After another long wait, I took off in a puff only to find nothing at all and slope land for a hot slog up. The others still up hadn’t even bothered launching. I guess I should’ve drunk a lot more than the few sips I had. Nearly an hour later, getting on 3pm, I had already decided it was going to be all or nothing when something more promising came through and we launched. Something weak worked in the gully W of TO and on the corner of Hawkswick. Ed, a visiting pilot and myself worked some broken somethings toward Hawkswick but I just couldn’t really pull it together. As Ed and ?? eventually climbed out, I finally admitted this clearly wasn’t my day. Strike 3 and Out.

I didn’t even attempt to land high anymore but landed below TO, packed up and walked back to the cars where by the time I got there some of the others were coming in to land.

The next evening I came down with a stomach bug. It may or may not have something to do with me being ‘off’ the day before.

Learning: Pay attention to your physical and mental state; sometimes it just isn’t your day. The hills will be there another day.

Fly Safe, Have Fun.

* BHPA incident report submitted

sections.title: The Four Peaks
sections.content:
Chris Kay reports
Convergence over Ingleborough

subsections.title: Ingleborough, July the 19th
subsections.content:
A climb takes me through the inversion above Ingleborough and very nearly over the back. XCTrack reckons 39 kmh drift and I spend five minutes slowly creeping forward on full bar before finding air that isn’t going up. To the south the ground is shaded out but a blue sky dotted with little fluffy clouds approaches from the north. So, without a better plan, or much of a plan at all, I head upwind.

The area around Ribblehead can be a sinkhole, but there are thermals today, some almost vertical with drift in single digits, whilst others have me retracing my path backwards for little gain in height. Out over the Old Hill Inn and past the viaduct and onto Blea Moor, I eventually find myself looking down into Dentdale where, running out of clouds to follow, I make a left turn to Great Coum and then another for the downwind leg back to Ingleborough, completing a triangle.

This short trip took three hours; enough fun for one day, I think, and set off for home via Penyghent, first crosswinding to the drumlins south of Ribblehead. Theory says that these egg-shaped hills are solar collectors, wind-shaded hollows and thermal triggers rolled into one and should be a good place to hunt for thermals. Sure enough, I find a climb here marked by a seagull and then another climb near Hull Pot gets me just shy of 6000 feet.

The last turns show 10kmh drift, which is within range for triangulation. Can I extend the circuit by flying back to Ingleborough? Heading north to the saddle between Penyghent and Plover Hill the wind is into the twenties but clouds over the valley work and I re-cross my track above Simon Fell with height to spare.

West of Ingleborough’s summit I reach 6300 feet in convergence and, with a northeasterly at my back, I fly out into the Lune valley, watching the number on the unfinished triangle calculator slowly tick up. The return leg, however, seems likely to end as an unceremonious sledge ride to the ground until a thermal from the limestone benches gives me the height needed to close the flight.

Six hours to fly a 50 km triangle is hardly record breaking. But it was an enjoyable day’s parapenting and it might just be the first tour of the summits of Ingleborough, Penyghent, Whernside and Great Coum —The Four Peaks.

Link to the flight on the XCLeague

sections.title: Club Nights – 2026/2027
sections.content:
Mike Barker reports

Following the positive feedback from last season, we'll be continuing our revised club night format.

Join us from 7:00pm in the bar area of the Horse n Farrier in Otley for pre-drinks and parachat—a great opportunity for new members to meet fellow pilots and socialise before the evening begins. Presentations will start at 7:30pm in the function room and will last up to 90 minutes, including a refreshment break halfway through. Afterwards, there'll be plenty of time to catch up with friends, enjoy the live music downstairs, or head home if you've got a long drive or work the next day.

The Horse & Farrier kindly provides the function room free of charge, so please support them where you can, thank the staff, and treat the venue with courtesy and respect.

This year's programme has been put together with the aim of offering something for everyone—new pilots, rusty pilots, nervous pilots, and even the sky gods looking to sharpen their skills. All of the talks below are confirmed for the 2026/27 season, so pop the dates in your diary and come along!

Thursday 1st October

The Northern Challenge Series – Winter Edition
 An exciting new winter version of the Northern Challenge Series, designed to help keep both new and experienced pilots current and motivated throughout the quieter months.
With thanks to Ed Cleasby.

Thursday 5th November

British Accuracy Pilots Academy
 With recent discussions about landing incidents on social media, this is an excellent opportunity to improve your landing skills. Who knows—you might even be tempted to have a go at the competitions!
With thanks to Andy Shaw and the British Accuracy Cup.

Thursday 3rd December

AGM & Awards Night
 Our annual AGM, followed by the presentation of trophies and the ever-coveted DHPC mugs.
With thanks to the DHPC Committee.

Thursday 7th January

Sports Psychology for Paraglider Pilots
 Fear, anxiety and pressure are all part of flying in a harness supported by string attached to some nylon. This talk explores how these psychological demands affect us, how they manifest physiologically, and practical strategies for managing them. It will also cover improving decision-making, confidence, consistency and performance—for the sky gods among us as well!
With thanks to Michael Deaville, Sports Psychologist, Leeds Beckett University.

Thursday 4th February

Astronomy for Pilots (by popular demand!)
 Perfect for those bivvying out under the stars—or anyone who missed Brian Cox's Arena tour. A fascinating guide to the night sky, our solar system, and why we're all essentially made from stardust… or perhaps nuclear waste!
With thanks to Mike Barker (who claims to know more about this than paragliding!).

Thursday 4th March

SIV?! – Simulation d'Incident en Vol (simulation of in-flight incidents)
 A group discussion on SIV experiences, with pilots sharing lessons learned from their first course through to those with many SIVs under their wings. A chance to learn from others' experiences and ask plenty of questions.

Thursday 1st April

Video Night
 An informal evening reviewing real flying incidents captured on camera, covering take-offs, in-flight situations and landings. We'll draw on the themes from previous talks to discuss what happened, what can be learned, and how we can all become safer and more confident pilots. The emphasis is firmly on learning, improving and sharing experiences.
With thanks to the DHPC Committee.

Further details on each talk will be published closer to the dates:

My thanks in advance to all of our speakers for generously giving up their time to make this programme possible. I always welcome constructive feedback, so if you have any ideas, suggestions, or potential speakers for the 2027/28 season, please let me know!

See you on a hill,

Mike Barker
DHPC Social Secretary
